Who sets and who collects Montgomery County property tax?

Two offices split the work: the State Department of Assessments and Taxation (SDAT) sets the value, and the county Department of Finance bills and collects. Maryland's 23 counties, Baltimore City and 155 incorporated municipalities issue the bills, and each level of government sets its own rate.

OfficeRoleContact
SDAT Montgomery County Assessment OfficeValues, notices, appeals30 W. Gude Drive, Suite 400, Rockville; (240) 314-4510
County Department of FinanceBilling and collection, tax lien sale101 Monroe Street, 15th Floor, Rockville; 240-777-8860
MC311Tax questions(240) 777-0311

Bills go out in July or August for the fiscal year that starts July 1. The Finance page also lists a tax credit for residents 65 and older and for retired military service members, and an online portal to view or pay real property bills.

What is the Montgomery County property tax rate?

The county's general property tax rate was 1.0392 in both FY 2025 and FY 2026, according to the Department of Legislative Services rate table. Those rates run on assessed value, and the full bill also carries state and other charges. The table lists the county rate history this way:

Fiscal yearCounty rate listed
FY 20220.9905
FY 20230.9915
FY 20241.0402

A table note adds that special rates apply for services not funded from the general county rate, so a given street can pay more or less than the headline number. The county did not raise the rate for the year that began July 1, 2026, but Montgomery Community Media reported on July 16, 2026 that many homeowners would still see higher bills.

Why might a Montgomery County tax bill go up when the rate did not?

Two changes pushed bills up in 2026: rising assessments and the end of a county credit. The Income Tax Offset Credit, shown on bills as the County Property Tax Credit, was $692 in levy year 2025. The County Council set it to $0 for 2026. It was not permanently repealed, and it only ever applied to owner-occupied principal residences.

The same report says the average county homeowner faces about $23 more per month from higher assessments. If the council sets the credit above zero again, a homeowner needs a homestead application on file with SDAT by May 1, 2027 for it to appear on July 1, 2027 bills.

Sellers should keep in mind that the credit amount is set year by year, so an old tax bill is a poor guide to what a buyer will pay.

How does the assessment cycle work in Montgomery County?

SDAT reappraises every property once every three years, so about one-third of Montgomery County homes get a new value each year. SDAT says an owner who thinks the total market value on the notice is wrong can appeal, and it never charges a fee for filing.

Montgomery Community Media notes that taxable assessment increases on a principal residence are capped at 10% per year, or 5% in the Town of Kensington. The state homestead credit works only for owner-occupied principal residences, and counties and towns pick a percentage between 0% and 10%.

The Department of Legislative Services estimates that the 10% cap costs Montgomery County 0.4% of its assessable base in the fiscal 2026 table. The cap does not apply in the first year after a purchase, so a long-time owner and a new neighbor can be taxed on different figures.

How do I appeal a Montgomery County assessment, and by when?

You have 45 days from the date on the SDAT notice to appeal a reassessment. SDAT's appeal process page lays out three steps. The Appeals Board charges no fee:

  1. The Supervisor's level, an informal hearing with an assessor that usually lasts about 15 minutes. SDAT supplies a property worksheet and area sales listing beforehand.
  2. The Property Tax Assessment Appeals Board, with one board in each of the 24 jurisdictions, appointed by the Governor and independent of SDAT.
  3. The Maryland Tax Court, which hears the case fresh and requires an in-person appearance.
StepDeadline
Appeal a reassessment notice45 days from notice date
Appeal to the Appeals Board30 days from the final Supervisor's notice
Appeal to the Tax Court30 days from the Board's order
New owner appeal60 days from transfer

A new owner appeal is open only for a transfer after January 1 and before July 1, and the deed must be recorded in the land records first. A seller closing in that window should tell the buyer about this option.

When are Montgomery County property taxes due?

Owners of a principal residence can pay in two installments, due September 30 and December 31. Other owners are on the single annual schedule, due without interest on July 1 and overdue after October 1.

The semiannual plan costs extra: local governments may add a service charge of up to 1.65% of the second payment. Fees on the same bill, such as water and sewer, may be due with the first installment.

Those who qualify for relief should look at two programs. The state Homeowners' Property Tax Credit is income-based and needs a new application every year. SDAT was accepting 2026 applications through October 1. The county senior credit equals 50% of the combined state credit and county supplement for residents 65 and older, and it also requires the state application.

What happens if Montgomery County taxes go unpaid?

Unpaid taxes become a lien, and the county sells the lien at an annual sealed-bid sale. The 2026 sale ran on Monday, June 8, 2026, and owners could stop a property from being sold by paying everything owed, with interest and penalties, by the last business day before the sale, Friday, June 5.

After a sale, the owner keeps the house and can redeem the lien until a Circuit Court order finally forecloses that right. Redemption interest on the certificate is 6% a year for owner-occupied properties and 20% a year for non-owner-occupied ones. A purchaser can seek foreclosure after 6 months, or 9 months for owner-occupied homes.

The state's tax sale survey gives a sense of scale for the 2024 sales:

MeasureMontgomery County
Properties advertised in first notice2,092
Offered for sale1,327
Liens sold1,029
Redeemed before foreclosure (FY 2024)1,184

The state also runs a Homeowner Protection Program and a Tax Sale Ombudsman, reachable at (410) 767-4994, for limited-income, elderly and disabled homeowners.

How do taxes show up when a Montgomery County house sells?

The unpaid balance is a lien on the house, so it has to be cleared for a clean transfer. A seller with back taxes should get a payoff figure from the Department of Finance, because penalties and interest keep running while the balance is open.

Closing also brings recordation and transfer tax, which the county reshaped in 2023. The guide to Montgomery County land records covers those charges. Deferred taxes under the optional program for owners 65 and older become a lien and are repaid when the property is transferred, according to SDAT's guide for homeowners.

Frequently asked questions

Who do I call about a Montgomery County property tax bill?

Start with MC311 at (240) 777-0311 or the Department of Finance at 240-777-8860. Questions about a value or appeal go to the SDAT Montgomery County assessment office at (240) 314-4510.

How long do I have to appeal a Montgomery County assessment?

You have 45 days from the date on the SDAT notice. A new owner who bought between January 1 and July 1 has 60 days from the transfer, once the deed is recorded.

When are Montgomery County property taxes due?

Principal residences can pay in two installments due September 30 and December 31. The semiannual plan can carry a service charge of up to 1.65% on the second payment.

Is there a cap on how fast my Montgomery County assessment can rise?

Yes. Taxable assessment increases on a principal residence are capped at 10% a year, or 5% in the Town of Kensington, and the cap does not apply in the first year after a purchase.

What is the redemption interest after a Montgomery County tax lien sale?

It is 6% a year for owner-occupied properties and 20% a year for non-owner-occupied properties, as stated on the certificate of sale. The owner can redeem until a court order forecloses the right.

Baltimore County versus Baltimore City

Baltimore County wraps around the independent city of Baltimore without including it. Towson is the county seat, and the 2020 census counted 854,535 residents across 682 square miles. The city left the county in 1851, so the offices described here serve only properties on the county side of the line. Baltimore City runs its own tax and land records offices. Communities range from dense Dundalk, Catonsville and Essex to a rural north, so lot size and property type vary widely.

2026 reassessment

SDAT revalued the county for January 1, 2026, and full cash value rose 12.1 percent over the three years from January 1, 2023.

MeasureJan. 1, 2023 valueJan. 1, 2026 valueChange
Combined value$47.17 billion$52.88 billionUp 12.1%
Residential$34.02 billion$38.22 billionUp 12.4%
Commercial$13.16 billion$14.65 billionUp 11.3%

About 85.93 percent of residential properties went up. An increase phases in evenly over three years, and a decrease applies fully in the 2026 tax year. The window to appeal is 45 days from the Notice of Assessment. SDAT hears it first, and further appeals go to the county board and then the Maryland Tax Court. SDAT keeps an office at 300 East Joppa Road, Room 602, in Towson.

How and when to pay

Real property tax bills are issued July 1. Owner-occupied homes can pay in two installments, the first through September 30 and the second through December 31. The county's schedule shows July 1 and December 1 as installment dates, with September 30 and December 31 as the last days to pay with no penalty or interest.

Owner-occupied homes and small businesses can use two-payment billing, provided the owner lives in the house for over six months out of twelve. Each installment covers half of the state and county tax, half of the homestead and homeowners' credits, and half of any metropolitan charges. If a mortgage escrow pays the first installment, no December bill is issued, but you still need to make sure the second payment goes out on time. To remain an annual payer, tell the mortgage company 60 days before the tax year.

The Office of Budget and Finance is at 400 Washington Avenue, Room 150, Towson, open Monday through Friday, 8 a.m. to 4:30 p.m. Call 410-887-2404 or email financeinfo@baltimorecountymd.gov.

The tax sale calendar

An unpaid bill can end with the property sold at the annual June tax sale. A missed first installment makes the account delinquent, and so does any balance left after December 31.

  • February: delinquent notices go out, and partial payments are taken until month end.
  • End of February: last day to apply for the Hardship Installment Payment Program and avoid a sale.
  • March 1: a Final Tax Sale notice gives 30 days to pay.
  • Around May 1: properties scheduled for sale are posted on the county website.
  • June: the annual tax sale.

The county gives an owner six months from the sale date to redeem. Ask the county and a lawyer how redemption and interest apply to your account. Partial payments do not stop interest, though they usually reduce what builds up.

Lien certificates

A lien certificate shows the status of unpaid taxes or charges on a property account, and the county requires one before any real property transfer. The fee is $55, payable to Baltimore County, Maryland, with a completed application. In most cases every unpaid tax and charge must be paid before the transfer goes through.

Order it early. The Transfer Tax Section at 410-887-2416 answers account questions, and the Liens Section of the Clerk of the Court at 410-887-2622 handles legal liens that show up on credit reports. Our Baltimore County land records guide covers the recording side of the same sale.

Selling a rental property

Every rental in the county needs a rental license or an exemption license under County Code Section 35-5-201, and the owner needs the license in hand before a tenant moves in. The rule covers dwellings of six or fewer units, short-term rentals included, and buildings with seven or more units.

  • Licenses last three years and can be renewed for further three-year terms.
  • Short-term rental licenses cost $300 per unit.
  • For seven or more units, an owner with fewer than three code violations in three years may file a self-certification affidavit. Otherwise 10 percent of units are inspected.
  • Within one mile of the main Towson University campus, licenses may be restricted where the rental rate is 30 percent or more.

Rental Housing Registration is at 111 West Chesapeake Avenue, Room 216, Towson, 410-887-6060. If you are selling a house with tenants, check that the license is current first.

Delinquent accounts and what to do first

If your account has gone delinquent, timing matters more than anything else. Partial payments are accepted through the end of February, and the Hardship Installment Payment Program application closes at the end of that month. After March 1 the clock is the 30 days on the Final Tax Sale notice, and by about May 1 the county posts the properties scheduled for the June sale.

Gather your bills, any notices you received and your mortgage statement before you call 410-887-2404. Tell the office whether the home is owner-occupied, since that decides whether the two-installment schedule applied to you. If a mortgage escrow was supposed to cover the first installment, ask the lender to confirm it was paid, because no December bill is issued in that case.

Selling with taxes owed

Because the county wants a lien certificate before transfer, plan to learn your balance early. The title company pays what is owed from the sale proceeds. If you have already received a Final Tax Sale notice, you have 30 days to pay from the March 1 mailing, so contact the Office of Budget and Finance right away.

  1. Order the lien certificate and check the amount.
  2. Ask the Transfer Tax Section whether any legal lien is attached.
  3. If you rent the house, confirm the license is current.
  4. Give the certificate to the title company so it can plan the payoff.

Keep every receipt and confirmation from the county, since the title company may ask for proof of what you have already paid, and note that a legal lien showing on a credit report is handled by the Clerk of the Court rather than the tax office. Clearing both before closing avoids surprises at the table.

A cash sale as is can move quickly. Send us the address and your balance, and we will tell you what we can offer.

Frequently asked questions

When are Baltimore County property taxes due?

Bills are issued July 1, and the first installment of a semiannual bill is payable through September 30. The second is payable through December 31 without penalty or interest.

Who can pay Baltimore County property tax in two installments?

Owner-occupied residential property and small businesses qualify. The owner must live in the home more than six months of a 12-month period.

How much is a Baltimore County lien certificate?

The fee is $55, payable to Baltimore County, Maryland, with a completed application. One is required before any real property transfer.

When is the Baltimore County tax sale?

The annual sale is in June. The county mails a Final Tax Sale notice on March 1 and posts properties on its website around May 1.

How long do I have to appeal a Baltimore County assessment?

You have 45 days from the Notice of Assessment to appeal to SDAT. The appeal then continues to the county appeals board and the Maryland Tax Court.

Anne Arundel County at a glance

Just south of Baltimore, Anne Arundel County fronts the Chesapeake Bay, and its seat Annapolis doubles as Maryland's capital. About 588,261 people lived here in 2020. Water covers 173 of the county's 588 square miles (29 percent), which is why creeks, rivers and shoreline lots define so much of the housing. Fort Meade, BWI airport and state government keep buyers coming, and commuters reach Baltimore and Washington by road, light rail or MARC.

The latest reassessment

The state assessments office, SDAT, revalued the county as of January 1, 2026. Here is how much value moved over the three years.

Measure (Jan. 1, 2023 to Jan. 1, 2026)Anne Arundel County
Combined full cash value$46.52 billion to $53.53 billion (up 15.1%)
Residential value$31.23 billion to $36.24 billion (up 16.0%)
Commercial value$15.28 billion to $17.29 billion (up 13.1%)
Residential properties that rose in value98.98%

Higher values are spread in equal steps over three years, while a drop applies in full for the 2026 tax year. To contest a value, you have 45 days from the date on the Notice of Assessment. Start with SDAT, then go to the county's Property Tax Assessment Appeals Board, and last to the Maryland Tax Court. On a principal residence, the homestead credit holds down how fast taxable assessment can grow: 10 percent is the state ceiling, and some local governments set it lower.

Due dates and payment options

The annual bill goes out in July to the mailing address SDAT has on file. It is payable without interest starting July 1 and must be settled by September 30. If you live in the house as your principal residence, you may pay in two halves, the first by September 30 and the second by December 31.

The fiscal year 2027 bill, covering July 1, 2026 to June 30, 2027, carries a 0.87 percent service charge on whatever is left for the second installment. Maryland lets local governments charge up to 1.65 percent, so this county stays under the limit. A single payment by September 30 avoids the charge altogether.

  • The state portion is $0.112 per $100 of taxable assessment.
  • Addresses inside the City of Annapolis add $0.738 per $100.
  • If a lender escrows your taxes and you prefer a single annual payment, notify the lender by May 1.
  • A homestead credit application filed by December 31 starts working July 1 of the next year.

Before you estimate what you owe, ask the Real Property Tax Division which county rate applies to your address.

Who to contact

The Real Property Tax Division, 44 Calvert Street, Room 110, Annapolis, answers billing questions. Reach it Monday through Friday, 8:00 a.m. to 4:30 p.m., at (410) 222-1736 or realproperty@aacounty.org. Values and ownership records sit with SDAT.

  • Finance Department customer service: (410) 222-1144.
  • Land Records, for deeds and liens: (410) 222-1425.
  • SDAT, to change ownership or a mailing address: (410) 974-5709.
  • Cashier's offices, including the one in Glen Burnie, are open Monday through Friday, 8:00 a.m. to 4:00 p.m. Outside those hours, drop a sealed check in the yellow box and it is handled the next business day.

Did you pay a bill on a house you have already sold? Ask the office about a refund. Credits left after a bill is adjusted are returned as quickly as possible.

Transfer and recordation taxes

Recording a deed here costs a county recordation tax of $7.00 per thousand of value, with the base rounded up to the next $500. The county transfer tax is 1.0 percent for prices through $999,999.99 and 1.5 percent from $1 million up. The Recordation and Transfer Tax Division collects both and must endorse any instrument that could be taxed before it goes on record.

Make checks payable to Anne Arundel County. The state's transfer tax and recording fees run through the Land Records Office at (410) 222-1425, which also accepts e-recording. Refund claim forms for both taxes and an affidavit for certain transactions are posted by the county. The sales contract decides who pays which tax, so have your title company list each charge before you accept an offer.

Waterfront sellers and the Critical Area

Land and water within 1,000 feet of tidal waters make up the Critical Area, and the rules can limit what a buyer is allowed to do with a lot.

  • The Buffer extends 100 feet landward from tidal waters, tributary stream banks and tidal wetland boundaries. Disturbing it generally takes an approved variance.
  • Removing any tree or vegetation, even a dead tree, requires an approved Vegetation Management Plan.
  • Grading disturbances over 5,000 square feet need a grading permit.
  • In limited development and resource conservation areas, impervious surface is capped at 15 to 31 percent of the site.

The county's Critical Area Planner of the Day is at the Heritage Complex, 2664 Riva Road, Annapolis, (410) 222-7960. Own a pier, deck or bulkhead near the water? Gather its permits before you list, and ask the title company whether any disclosure applies.

If taxes go unpaid

Tax left unpaid turns into a lien, and the county can auction that lien at its June tax sale on a date the Controller picks. You still own the house afterward. The winning bidder gets a tax lien certificate and may foreclose if the debt is never cleared.

Ahead of the sale the collector has to mail you a notice at least 30 days before the first advertisement, which then runs weekly for four weeks. The buyer can start foreclosure six months after the sale, or nine for an owner-occupied home, and the certificate dies if nothing is filed within two years. To redeem, you pay interest of 1.5 percent per month, so every month of delay adds to the payoff.

Homeowners with limited income, or who are elderly or disabled, may be eligible for the state's Homeowner Protection Program. The State Tax Sale Ombudsman sees people by appointment at 123 Market Place, Baltimore.

Selling with taxes owed

Owing money to the county does not block a sale, as long as the balance is cleared by closing. Get the amount from the Real Property Tax Division, and move before the June tax sale if you are behind. The title company can wire the county out of your proceeds.

  1. Request a payoff figure for each open bill.
  2. Collect permits for any waterfront structures and any Critical Area approvals.
  3. Have the title company spell out the recordation and transfer taxes.
  4. Close, and the title company pays the county from the proceeds.

Our offers are for the house as it stands, so a worn bulkhead or an old deck is not something you have to fix first. Send the address by call or text and we will say what we can pay.

Frequently asked questions

When are Anne Arundel County property taxes due?

Payment without interest opens July 1 and closes September 30. A principal residence may be paid half by September 30 and half by December 31.

What is the semiannual service charge in Anne Arundel County?

It is 0.87 percent of the second installment balance for fiscal year 2027. One full payment by September 30 avoids it.

How do I appeal an Anne Arundel County assessment?

Send it to SDAT within 45 days of the Notice of Assessment. Still unhappy? Take it to the county appeals board, then the Maryland Tax Court.

What are the transfer tax rates in Anne Arundel County?

Transfer tax is 1.0 percent through $999,999.99 and 1.5 percent at $1 million or more. Recordation tax is $7.00 per thousand, rounded up to the next $500.

Does the Critical Area affect selling a house near the water?

It can. A lot within 1,000 feet of tidal water is in the Critical Area, with a 100 foot buffer plus vegetation and grading rules that a buyer needs to know about.

Where is Frederick County and how is it governed?

Frederick County is in north-central Maryland, in the Washington metropolitan area, with the city of Frederick as its seat. It borders Pennsylvania to the north, Carroll County to the east, Montgomery County to the south, Loudoun County, Virginia to the southwest and Washington County to the west.

At 667 square miles, with only 7.2 of them water, it is the largest Maryland county by land area. The county was founded June 10, 1748, and on December 1, 2014 it became a charter home rule government with a seven-member council and an elected county executive. Jessica Fitzwater has held that office since 2022.

Population was 271,717 in 2020, and Wikipedia gives a 2025 estimate of 302,883. Growth has been steady since the 1980s as people moved out from the Washington area.

What does the Frederick County landscape look like?

Frederick County straddles the Piedmont Plateau and the Appalachian Mountains, and its two main ridges, Catoctin Mountain and South Mountain, extend the Blue Ridge. The Middletown Valley lies between them.

That mix gives sellers very different properties:

  • City and suburban lots in and around Frederick and the county's smaller towns.
  • Valley farms in the Middletown Valley. The county leads Maryland in milk production, with dairy herds making up about a third of the state's total, though dairy farms have been closing.
  • Mountain parcels near Catoctin Mountain Park, which contains Camp David, and near the South Mountain battlefields.

Brunswick, Mount Airy, Emmitsburg and Thurmont have their own police departments, Middletown contracts with the Sheriff's Office, and fire and rescue draws on more than 450 career firefighters and about 300 volunteers across 26 corporations.

Fort Detrick is the largest employer in Frederick County, with 10,827 employees in the 2025 figures reported by Wikipedia. The next five are listed below.

When are Frederick County property tax bills due?

Annual and first semiannual bills are due September 30, and the second semiannual installment is due December 31. Bills are mailed in July and posted online by July 1.

  • Early payment discount: 1 percent for payments received in July and one-half percent in August, on annual and semiannual bills.
  • Interest: accrues on unpaid accounts from October 1 at 1 percent per month.
  • Supplemental bills: mailed in August for June transfers and state credits issued after the July billing. Supplemental and revised bills are due 30 days from issue.
  • Postmark rule: USPS payments postmarked by the last calendar day of the month are credited as of the postmark date. Electronic payments must be entered by midnight on the last day.

The county says that failing to receive a bill does not excuse payment. Mortgage companies do not receive bills; they use an electronic file. Homeowners who escrow must send new construction bills to their lender, because those go only to the owner.

Where do you pay Frederick County property tax?

The Frederick County Treasury Department is at 30 North Market Street in Frederick, open 8 a.m. to 4 p.m., Monday to Friday, and its number is 301-600-1111. The office takes cash, checks, money orders and cards in person.

Card payments are processed through a vendor with a 2.5 percent fee, and the county says it receives none of that fee. The mailing address is the Treasury Department at 30 N. Market St., Frederick, MD 21701. Lenders can use a mass payment option through the billing office.

The county's Treasury page also offers Lien Certificate and Tax Status Report requests. Ordering one before closing shows what tax, if any, is still open.

What rates and local taxes apply in Frederick County?

Unincorporated Frederick County had a real property rate of 1.1100 per $100 of assessed value in fiscal 2025, and the same rate is shown for fiscal 2026. The rate was 1.0600 from fiscal 2022 to 2024.

State tables list a Frederick County transfer tax of 0.0 percent and a recordation tax figure of $7.00 for fiscal 2025 and 2026. Each municipality also levies its own district tax for services such as streets, trash removal and police. Homestead credit caps vary by municipality from 0 percent to 10 percent.

The county page lists these relief programs:

  • Senior Tax Credit: for owners 65 or older who meet income limits, equal to 20 percent of net county real property taxes.
  • Deferral program: for owners of at least five years who are 65 or older or totally disabled and meet income limits. Deferred amounts become a lien at 3 percent annual interest.
  • Homestead Tax Credit: limits yearly taxable assessment increases on a principal residence, applied automatically after 12 months of residence. Call SDAT at 301-815-5350.
  • Homeowner's Property Tax Credit: income based for all ages, with applications due by September of the tax year.

How can you appeal a Frederick County assessment?

Frederick County owners appeal to the Supervisor of Assessments within 45 days of the notice date, then to the Property Tax Assessment Appeals Board within 30 days, then to the Maryland Tax Court within 30 days. Both the board and the Tax Court have no filing fee.

Notices come about every three years. In the two years between, a petition for review is due by the first working day after January 1. Hearings at the first level can be written, by phone, by video or in person. If you bought a house transferred between January 1 and June 30, you can appeal within 60 days of the transfer once the deed is recorded.

What if Frederick County tax goes unpaid or the house needs repairs?

Frederick County sells tax liens online, and the state's 2026 schedule lists the county on May 11. An owner can redeem until the Circuit Court forecloses the right.

The county says an owner keeps possession during redemption. Redemption without added expenses such as legal fees is possible during the first four months for a non-owner-occupied property and the first seven months for an owner-occupied one. The certificate interest rate is 8 percent a year. Call 301-600-1111 for the redemption amount.

Rental condition is a separate matter. The county replaced its Minimum Livability Code with the 2024 International Property Maintenance Code, effective June 6, 2026, and the Division of Housing at 401 Sagner Avenue enforces it on complaint. Complaints for properties inside the city of Frederick go to city inspectors at 301-600-3825.

Frequently asked questions

September 30 for annual bills and the first semiannual installment, and December 31 for the second. Interest of 1 percent per month starts October 1 on unpaid accounts. Payments in July earn a 1 percent discount and August payments earn one-half percent.

How do I reach the Frederick County Treasury?

Call 301-600-1111 or visit 30 North Market Street in Frederick, Monday to Friday from 8 a.m. to 4 p.m. The office accepts cash, checks, money orders and cards.

What is the Frederick County property tax rate?

The fiscal 2025 and 2026 county rate is 1.1100 per $100 of assessed value in the unincorporated area, according to the Department of Legislative Services. Municipalities add their own rates, so a house inside a town pays more.

Can I sell a Frederick County house with unpaid property tax?

Yes, the title company can pay unpaid tax from the proceeds at closing. Ask the Treasury for a lien certificate or tax status report so the payoff amount is clear before you set a closing date.

Does Frederick County charge a transfer tax?

The state's local tax table shows a 0.0 percent county transfer tax and a $7.00 recordation tax figure for fiscal 2025 and 2026. State-level charges may still apply, so check the closing statement with the title company.

Where is Howard County and what does it include?

Howard County is in central Maryland between Baltimore and Washington, D.C., and it is the smallest county in the state by total area. It covers 253 square miles, with only 2.7 of them water, and it sits on the Piedmont Plateau.

The Patapsco River forms its northern and northeastern edge, and the Patuxent River forms the southwestern one. The Triadelphia and Rocky Gorge reservoirs lie along the Patuxent. Howard has no incorporated towns at all, so the county government handles services that a city would elsewhere.

The two names most sellers recognize are Columbia and Ellicott City. Columbia is a planned community founded in 1967 with roughly 100,000 residents. Ellicott City is the county seat and, with 75,947 residents in 2020, is described as the most populous unincorporated county seat in the country.

Because there is no municipal layer, a Howard deed goes through one county finance office rather than a town clerk first.

What is the history behind Howard County and Ellicott City?

Howard County is named for John Eager Howard, a Continental Army colonel who commanded at Cowpens and later served as Maryland's fifth governor. Encyclopedia sources disagree on the exact founding date, giving 1838 in one place and July 4, 1851 in another, so it is safest to cite the county's own materials for a date.

Ellicott City began with three Quaker brothers, John, Andrew and Joseph Ellicott, who picked the mill site on April 24, 1771. Ellicott's Mills grew into one of the larger milling towns in the East. The Ellicott City Historic District has been listed since 1973, and the 1830 Ellicott City Station is called the oldest surviving railroad station in the United States.

Columbia is the opposite story, laid out in 1967 as a single plan.

What does Howard County's economy look like?

Howard County has a high-income, high-education economy. Median household income was estimated at $124,042 in 2020, and about 63.6% of adults 25 and older hold a bachelor's degree or higher.

How do roads and travel shape selling a house in Howard County?

Interstate 95 crosses the eastern part of Howard County and Interstate 70 crosses the north. Maryland Route 32 runs through Clarksville, Glenelg and Glenwood in the western half.

  • No commercial airport sits inside the county.
  • BWI, Reagan National and Dulles all serve it.
  • Merriweather Post Pavilion and Savage Mill are among the notable local attractions.

What flood risk does Ellicott City carry?

Ellicott City's historic core sits where several stream valleys meet, and it has flooded badly twice in recent years. On July 30, 2016 about 6 inches of rain fell in two hours and two people died. On May 27, 2018 more than 8 inches fell in two hours and one person died.

The county settled on a roughly $140 million, five-year plan that included a 15-foot-diameter tunnel through about 1,600 feet of hillside. The stated goal was to cut street flooding from more than four feet to under one foot, not to remove flooding entirely. Building removals and construction ran from January 2024 into summer 2024, and renovation of six remaining buildings was still underway in February 2025.

If your house is in or near the historic district, expect buyers and lenders to ask about flood history and insurance. Elsewhere in the county the same question comes up for homes beside streams.

Who bills Howard County property tax and how much is the rate?

The Howard County Department of Finance bills real property tax each July 1, and SDAT sets the assessed value. The Finance phone line is 410-313-2062.

SDAT's 2026 to 2027 table lists a county real property rate of $1.0440 per $100 and a State rate of $0.1120, with a 5% homestead credit cap and no municipal rate. We use SDAT's line for the base rate, so confirm the full bill on your own tax account.

  • Prior-year bills and history: the county's self-service site.
  • E-check fee: $1.00. Card fee: 2.35%, with a $2.00 minimum.
  • Allow three to five business days for processing.

Many taxpayers can choose semiannual payments. The county page names property tax credits but lists none, so ask the office what applies to you.

How does a Howard County assessment appeal work?

A reassessment appeal must be filed within 45 days of the date printed on the notice. SDAT mails a Notice of Assessment about every three years, so most owners get one every third year and none in between.

The first step is an informal hearing at the Supervisor's level, usually around 15 minutes. If you disagree with the result, you can take the case to the local Property Tax Assessment Appeals Board within 30 days, and then to the Maryland Tax Court within 30 days of the board's order. Neither the board nor the court charges a filing fee.

In the two years between notices, a petition for review is due by the first working day after January 1. If the house transfers after January 1 and before July 1, a purchase appeal can be filed within 60 days of the transfer.

What transfer and recordation costs apply to a Howard County sale?

A Howard County deed carries a State transfer tax of 0.5%, a county transfer tax of 1.25% and a recordation tax of $2.50 per $500 of consideration. The Clerk of the Circuit Court lists all three on its Land Records page.

Every deed goes first to the Division of Recordation Tax, in the Howard County Department of Finance at 3430 Courthouse Drive in Ellicott City, then to Land Records at 9250 Judicial Way, Suite 1900. The recordation office is open 8 a.m. to 4:30 p.m. and answers at 410-313-2389. Land Records recording hours are 8:30 a.m. to 3:30 p.m.

The county says consideration is not limited to cash and can include debt a buyer assumes. Misstating it on a deed is a crime under the Tax-Property Article.

What if Howard County property tax is overdue at sale time?

Howard County holds one tax sale a year, and the 2026 sale took place on Wednesday, June 10. The county advertises delinquent properties in the Howard County Times for at least four weeks before the sale.

The State's tax sale report lists Howard with the shortest wait of any county in its table, 30 days overdue before a property can be offered. In 2024 the county advertised 1,103 parcels, offered 349 and sold 308, with 173 of those owner-occupied. Interest runs 1.5% a month on the county share and 1% on the State share, and redemption interest is 18% a year.

Bidders buy a tax lien certificate, not the house. An owner can redeem any time before a circuit judge signs a foreclosure order. Selling the house works because the payoff on the lien is paid at settlement from proceeds.

Real property tax is billed on July 1 each year. The county lets many owners choose two installments, and the Finance Department can confirm the dates on your bill.

The county transfer tax is 1.25% of the consideration. The State adds 0.5%, and recordation tax is $2.50 per $500.

Start at the Division of Recordation Tax, 3430 Courthouse Drive, Ellicott City, to pay county taxes and have the deed stamped. Then record at Land Records, 9250 Judicial Way, Suite 1900, or through e-recording.

Does Howard County have towns that set their own property tax?

No. Howard has no incorporated municipalities, and SDAT lists a municipal rate of 0.0000. All real property tax comes through the county and the State.

How long do I have to appeal a Howard County assessment?

You have 45 days from the notice date. After the supervisor's hearing, you have 30 days to go to the appeals board and 30 more days to reach the Maryland Tax Court.

What is Prince George's County, Maryland, and why does its geography matter for a tax bill?

Prince George's County sits on the eastern side of Washington, D.C., and covers about 499 square miles, of which 483 are land. The Patuxent River forms its eastern edge, and only South County touches the Potomac.

Residents and planners talk about five informal regions: North County, Central County, the Rural Tier, the Inner Beltway and South County. U.S. Route 50 is the broad line between north and south. The county seat is Upper Marlboro, and the county was created in 1696 from parts of Charles and Calvert counties.

Geography shows up on the bill in two ways. A house inside an incorporated city, such as Bowie, carries a municipal tax and gets a reduced county rate. A house in unincorporated land pays the county rate in full. Anyone selling should check which one applies before reading a bill.

Who lives and works in Prince George's County?

The 2020 census counted 967,201 people in the county, and the 2025 estimate is 970,374, which makes it the second most populous county in Maryland after Montgomery. The county has had a charter form of government since 1970, with nine council districts plus two at-large seats.

Federal employment shapes the local economy more than most counties. The figures below are 2021 employer counts reported on the county's Wikipedia entry.

For a seller, this means many owners have jobs tied to federal posts and transfers. A reassignment can force a sale on a short clock, which is one reason owners here look for a quick closing.

How do roads and rail connect the county's neighborhoods?

The county has 15 Washington Metro stations, and four of them are line ends: Greenbelt, New Carrollton, Largo and Branch Avenue. MARC commuter trains add five Camden Line stops and three Penn Line stops.

  • 28 miles of the Capital Beltway (I-495) run through the county.
  • An 11.5-mile stretch of the Baltimore-Washington Parkway lies inside its borders.
  • The Intercounty Connector opened in 2012.
  • The Purple Line is described as slated to open in 2027.

Distance to a Metro or MARC station is one of the first things a buyer checks, so it also affects how fast a house sells on the open market.

When is the Prince George's County property tax bill due?

The county issues bills every July, and full payment is due September 30. Late payments pick up interest and a penalty, and missing a bill does not excuse the owner.

Owner-occupied homes with a bill marked Principal Residence can pay in two equal parts, the first by September 30 and the second by December 31. Maryland lets local governments add a service charge of up to 1.65% to the second half, according to the state assessments department.

The county's Tax Facts guide gives the late charge as 1.67% per month. The tax year runs July 1 to June 30. Treat that figure as a reason to pay on time rather than a number to plan around.

What rates make up a Prince George's County bill?

A bill is built from several separate rates, each stated per $100 of assessed value. The county's Tax Facts guide lists these fiscal 2026 rates.

The county's own formula is simple: divide the assessment by 100, multiply by the rate, then add any charges. The guide also gives a constant yield rate of $0.9591 for tax year 2026 and a certified unincorporated assessable base of $86.5 billion.

Extra charges can appear on the same bill. Front Foot Benefit covers sewer or water pipes laid in the street (WSSC, 301-206-8032). Solid Waste Service pays for trash and waste programs (Department of the Environment, 301-952-7630). A tax lien charge appears when taxes or fines are in arrears.

How does a reassessment change what an owner pays?

The State Department of Assessments and Taxation sets values, and it reassesses each property every three years. The January 1, 2026 cycle raised residential values in Prince George's County by 10.3% compared with January 1, 2023, and notices went out on December 30, 2025.

Increases are phased in evenly over three years, and decreases take full effect in the 2026 tax year. Homestead and Homeowners' credits are also run by the state, and the county's own credits are listed on its Property Tax Credits page.

Disagreements start with the state assessments department, then go to the county Property Tax Assessment Appeals Board, then to the Maryland Tax Court. For a dwelling, the appeal board must hold a hearing within 120 days after receiving the request, unless the owner asks for a delay.

Email questions go to tax_inquiry@co.pg.md.us. When a house is being sold, the title company usually pays the bill from proceeds, so the seller only needs the current account balance.

What happens when taxes go unpaid in Prince George's County?

Real property taxes still unpaid by the second Monday in May are sold to the highest bidder at the county's annual tax sale. That sale turns a late bill into a lien held by a third party, so it is a real deadline.

Owners behind on taxes often find that a conventional listing is difficult, because lenders and title companies need the balance cleared at closing. A cash buyer can sometimes pay the arrears at settlement out of the price. Ask the Treasury Division for a payoff figure before you set a closing date.

What does a seller pay when the deed is recorded?

Maryland charges transfer and recordation taxes on a sale, and the rates differ by county. A 2026 staff table at the Maryland General Assembly lists Prince George's County at a 1.4% transfer tax and a recordation tax of $2.75 per $500 of consideration, both unchanged from fiscal 2022 through fiscal 2027. The City of Baltimore's finance office lists the state transfer tax as a separate 0.5% of consideration, which applies on top of the local rate.

Which side pays, and how the split is written, is set in the contract of sale. Confirm the exact amounts with the title company, since municipal and state add-ons differ by deal.

What local rules affect a Prince George's County house before it sells?

The county's Office of Homeland Security code compliance staff enforce housing, zoning and rental rules. Inspectors act on complaints or cleanup sweeps and issue a Notice of Violation, a Civil Citation or both, with a deadline to fix the problem.

  • Report a violation by calling 311 inside the county or 301-883-4748 outside it, Monday to Friday, 7:00 a.m. to 7:00 p.m.
  • A single-family rental needs a county license, valid for two years, unless the city or town licenses it instead. Bowie is among the municipalities the county does not license.
  • A license is refused when an inspector finds life-safety violations, including unpermitted construction or an illegal conversion.
  • Landlords who use a pre- or post-settlement occupancy agreement between buyer and seller are exempt from the license requirement.

A house with open citations or unpermitted work can lose bids, so a seller who cannot fix them in time may prefer an as-is sale.

What must a Prince George's County seller disclose?

A seller of a one- to four-unit home must give the buyer a disclosure or a disclaimer statement on or before signing the contract, under Maryland Real Property Code section 10-702. The disclaimer form says the home is sold as-is, apart from known latent defects.

Several sales are exempt, including bank sales after foreclosure, sheriff and tax sales, and transfers by fiduciaries in estates and trusts. A buyer who did not get the statement in time can rescind within five days after receiving it, and the right cannot be waived in the contract.

Frequently asked questions

When is Prince George's County property tax due?

Full payment is due September 30, and bills go out each July. Owner-occupied homes marked Principal Residence can split it into September 30 and December 31 installments.

Where is the Prince George's County Treasury Division?

The customer counter is at 1301 McCormick Drive, Suite 1100, Largo, MD 20774, open 9:00 a.m. to 4:00 p.m. on weekdays. Call 301-952-4030 for help.

Can I pay Prince George's County property tax with cash?

No, the county says cash is not accepted at its counter. It takes checks, money orders and cashier's checks in person, plus cards and e-checks online with fees.

When does the Prince George's County tax sale happen?

Taxes unpaid by the second Monday in May are sold to the highest bidder at the annual tax sale. Contact Treasury before then for a payoff figure.

What is the Prince George's County transfer tax rate?

A 2026 General Assembly staff table lists 1.4% for the county, with a $2.75 recordation rate per $500. The state adds its own 0.5% transfer tax, so confirm totals with the title company.

Who sets my assessment in Prince George's County?

The Maryland State Department of Assessments and Taxation does. Reassessment happens every three years, and the January 1, 2026 cycle raised residential values by 10.3%.

Does Bowie get its rental license from the county?

No. The county says Bowie is among the municipalities it does not license, so landlords apply with the city.

Where is Harford County and how is it laid out?

How do roads and transit affect a Harford County house sale?

U.S. Route 40 is the county's main east and west road, and other arteries lead toward Baltimore. Commuters from Edgewood and Aberdeen can use the MARC Penn Line, which stops in both places. Harford Transit runs county buses, and Harford County Airport in Churchville handles small general aviation.

  • Road: U.S. Route 40 and the other Baltimore-bound arteries.
  • Air: Harford County Airport in Churchville, general aviation only.
  • Bus: Harford Transit, run by the county.

The Conowingo Dam sits on the county's eastern border, and the Susquehanna flows past it into the bay.

Who bills Harford County property tax and what is the rate?

The Harford County Department of the Treasury bills and collects real estate tax, while the State Department of Assessments and Taxation (SDAT) sets the value. The Treasury is at 220 S. Main Street in Bel Air, and tax payments can go through 410-638-3269 or treasury@harfordcountymd.gov.

The county rate has been steady for several years. The Maryland Department of Legislative Services lists the county rate at $0.9779 per $100 of assessed value for fiscal years 2023 through 2027. SDAT's 2026 to 2027 table adds the State rate of $0.1120 and shows a 5% homestead credit cap.

How do you appeal a Harford County assessment?

You have 45 days from the date on your Notice of Assessment to file a reassessment appeal. SDAT sends that notice about every three years, and you can file online with the control number on the notice or return the paper form to the local assessment office.

  • Supervisor's level: an informal hearing, usually about 15 minutes, by writing, phone, video or in person.
  • Property Tax Assessment Appeals Board: file within 30 days of the final notice. No fee.
  • Maryland Tax Court: file within 30 days of the board's order. Hearings are in person and start fresh.
  • Petition for review: for the two years between reassessments, filed by the first working day after January 1.
  • Purchase appeal: if the property transfers after January 1 and before July 1, file within 60 days of the transfer.

Tax owed at settlement is the billed amount, so an appeal in progress does not change the payoff figure.

What does Harford County require before a deed can be transferred?

Harford County requires a Certificate of Tax Liens and Other Charges Due before a transfer. The county charges $50 by check payable to Harford County Government, and the certificate is valid for 90 days from the date of issue. It covers real estate tax, water and sewer special assessments and other charges.

Title companies usually order it, but an owner selling alone can apply by mailing the form to Bureau of Revenue Collections, P.O. Box 609, Bel Air, MD 21014. The county's page gives no processing time.

State law also asks for proof that charges are paid. Under Real Property Article 3-104, taxes and assessments due must be paid, with the collector's certificate endorsed on the deed, before the transfer goes on the assessment books.

County staff also stamp every deed before it is recorded, whether or not tax is owed. Drop-off is at the Revenue Collections Office, Monday to Friday, 8 a.m. to 5 p.m., and the county says processing usually takes 24 to 48 hours.

What transfer and recordation taxes apply to a Harford County sale?

A Harford County deed carries a 1% county transfer tax, a recordation tax of $6.60 per $1,000 of value and a 0.5% State transfer tax. Proceeds from the county transfer tax are split evenly between farmland preservation and school costs.

Recordation tax at $6.60 per $1,000 works out to $3.30 per $500, which matches the Department of Legislative Services table. The Circuit Court collects the State transfer tax, and Revenue Collections collects the county pieces.

  • Recording fee for most deeds of nine pages or less: $20, plus a $40 surcharge.
  • Land Records is at 20 West Courtland Street, Bel Air, open 8:30 a.m. to 4:30 p.m.
  • E-recording runs through Simplifile.
  • Tax exemptions must cite the full exemption code on the document or full tax is charged.

Who pays each tax is set by contract. Absent an agreement, the law presumes recordation and transfer taxes are split equally, with an exception when the buyer is a first-time Maryland buyer who will live in the house.

What happens when Harford County property tax goes unpaid?

Unpaid Harford County tax becomes eligible for the annual tax sale about three months after it is overdue. In 2024 the sale was held in June, the county advertised 1,044 parcels owing about $2.33 million, and 282 parcels sold.

Interest builds at 1.5% a month on the county portion and 1% a month on the State portion, starting October 1 for a bill that was not paid by September 30. The county's page says tax-sale preparation charges are added from May 1. Winning bidders buy a lien, not the house, so the owner stays the owner and can redeem by paying the lien, interest and fees.

The State's 2025 tax sale report says an owner may redeem any time before a circuit judge signs a foreclosure order. The earliest a purchaser may file to foreclose that right in most counties is six months after the sale. Harford reported an installment plan under Tax-Property Article 10-209 and listed annual redemption interest of 12%.

The Harford County Department of the Treasury sends it, usually mailed on July 1. SDAT sets the assessed value, and the county adds its rate. Questions about payment go to 410-638-3269.

Can I sell a house in Harford County with back taxes owed?

Yes. The unpaid balance, interest and any tax-sale charges are paid from the sale proceeds at settlement, and the county's lien certificate shows the figure. You still need to move before the annual sale if you want to avoid a lien auction.

How long is the Harford County lien certificate good for?

It is valid for 90 days from the date of issue. The application fee is $50, and the request goes to the Bureau of Revenue Collections in Bel Air.

What is the Harford County transfer tax rate?

The county transfer tax is 1% of the consideration. The State adds 0.5%, or 0.25% for a first-time Maryland buyer who will occupy the house, and recordation tax is $6.60 per $1,000.

How do I contest my Harford County assessment?

File an appeal within 45 days of the notice date at SDAT. The next steps are the Property Tax Assessment Appeals Board and then the Maryland Tax Court, and neither charges a filing fee.

Where is Charles County and what is its layout?

Charles County sits in Southern Maryland, with La Plata as the county seat and Waldorf as its largest community. It is bordered by Prince George's County to the north, Calvert and St. Mary's counties to the east and southeast, and several Virginia counties across the Potomac.

The county covers 643 square miles, but only 458 of them are land. The other 185 square miles, about 29 percent, are water, which is why creeks, swamps and shoreline show up in so many property descriptions. Nanjemoy Creek and Zekiah Swamp are two of the named features.

Charles County was created in 1658 and named for Charles Calvert, the third Baron Baltimore. Its population was 166,617 in the 2020 census, and the 2025 estimate cited by Wikipedia is 176,593, up 6.0 percent.

What towns and areas do Charles County sellers deal with?

Most sellers here fall into one of four settings: Waldorf, La Plata, Indian Head or the rural south and west. Each has its own buyer pool and its own tax picture.

  • Waldorf: a census-designated place about 23 miles south-southeast of Washington, D.C. It had 81,410 residents in 2020, up from fewer than 5,000 in 1980, largely because of the planned community of St. Charles that began after a 1970 federal loan package. U.S. Route 301 is its main commercial road and Maryland Route 5 starts there.
  • La Plata: the county seat, where the April 28, 2002 tornado (rated F-4) destroyed much of downtown and killed three people.
  • Indian Head: a town tied to the naval installation on the Potomac, which is the county's largest employer.
  • Rural Charles: places such as Nanjemoy, Port Tobacco Village, Newburg and Bryantown, where lots are larger, wells and septic are common, and water is never far away.

What does flood risk mean for a Charles County house?

Charles County tries to keep its floodplain open so water can spread out and move downstream, and a house inside a mapped Special Flood Hazard Area is treated differently from one outside it. The county's floodplain page states plainly that homeowners insurance does not cover flood damage and that residents can buy a National Flood Insurance Program policy through an insurance agent.

With 29 percent of the county's total area in water, owners near the Potomac, creeks and swamps should expect a buyer's lender to ask about flood zone status. Check the FEMA map for the parcel before listing, and have any flood insurance paperwork ready. Flood status can also affect the price a buyer offers.

What happens if Charles County property tax goes unpaid?

Unpaid property tax in Maryland becomes a lien, and the county can sell that lien at public auction. The owner keeps the house, but the buyer gains the right to collect and eventually to ask a court to foreclose.

  • The collector mails a notice at least 30 days before the property is first advertised, and the listing runs weekly for four weeks.
  • An owner can redeem at any time until a court finally forecloses the right to redeem, and costs grow the longer the owner waits.

When a house is sold before that point, the title company normally pays the tax from the sale proceeds. The ombudsman's office can be reached at 410-767-4994, and its Homeowner Protection Program helps limited-income, elderly and disabled homeowners.

Yes. A sale can close with the tax paid out of the proceeds, and it can happen before a tax sale or while the lien is still open for redemption. The payoff amount changes with interest and fees, so ask the Treasurer or the title company for a current figure.

Does Charles County have a tax sale every year?

The county page says delinquent properties may be sold at the annual tax sale held each May, and the state's 2026 schedule shows May 12. A property is sold only if the account is still unpaid at that point.

The Treasurer's Office is at 150 Main Street, Prince Frederick, 410-535-1600. It handles tax liens and runs the annual tax sale.

Help for owners who are behind

The Homeowner Protection Program can pull a qualifying owner out of the tax sale process for three years. Requirements include a principal residence, an assessed value of $300,000 or less, household income of $60,000 or less, and non-dwelling assets of $200,000 or less.

The state Homeowners' Tax Credit is open to primary-residence owners with gross household income under $60,000, and applications go to the state. A Bay Restoration Fund hardship exemption lasts one year and must be renewed. These programs can lower what you owe before closing, and they can slow a tax sale long enough to list the house without a lien deadline hanging over you.

Building excise tax on new homes

Calvert charges a building excise tax on new residential construction, and it follows the property as a lien. A new single-family detached house totals $12,950, with $4,550 due at permit and $4,200 on each of the next two tax bills.

Other totals are $10,325 for a single-family attached unit, $9,050 for a manufactured home and $7,750 for an apartment. Later installments show up on the regular tax bill, so a buyer of a newly built home should ask whether any remain unpaid. The county enforces the tax like real property tax, with the same priority, interest and penalties for lien purposes. If you are selling a house built in the last two or three years, ask the Treasurer's Office what is left.

Roads, water and weather

Routes 4 and 2 meet at Sunderland and run together as Route 2-4, Solomons Island Road, through Prince Frederick, St. Leonard and Lusby. Route 260 runs southeast to Chesapeake Beach, and the Governor Thomas Johnson Bridge carries Route 4 into St. Mary's County. Summers are hot and humid and winters mild to chilly, so roofs and siding see the full range, and buyers of bay-side houses will look closely at both.

  • The tax ID number for your account, which the online portal uses to find your bills.
  • Your most recent bill, plus the one before it if a balance carries over.
  • Your mortgage servicer's name, if the lender pays from escrow.
  • For a newer house, the building permit date, so the office can tell you which excise installments are left.
  • Proof of income and assets if you want to ask about the Homeowner Protection Program or the state credit.

The office can tell you whether the account has been sent to tax sale. That single fact decides whether a partial payment is still possible, so ask it first.

Waterfront and older houses

Calvert's long shoreline means many sellers have docks, bulkheads, septic systems or houses close to the water. Buyers and their lenders ask about all of these, and a missing permit or an old system can slow a traditional sale. Collect whatever paperwork you have on repairs and upgrades. A cash offer is made on the house as it stands, so an aging septic tank or a tired deck is not something you have to resolve before closing, though the tax balance still gets paid from the proceeds.

Selling with tax due

  1. Look up the account on the county's online tax portal using the tax ID number.
  2. Ask the Treasurer's Office whether any amount has gone to tax sale, because partial payments stop once it has.
  3. Check your mortgage escrow so you do not pay twice.
  4. Ask the title company to order a payoff through your closing date.

If the house also needs repairs you cannot afford, selling as is lets unpaid tax come out of the proceeds at settlement instead of sitting on the account. Call or text us with the address and we will tell you what we can offer.

The county rate is $0.967 per $100 of assessed value, unchanged for fiscal 2027. With the state's $0.112, unincorporated areas pay $1.079 per $100.

When are Calvert County property taxes due?

Owners of a principal residence may pay in two installments due September 30 and December 31. The second carries a service charge.

What is the homestead cap in Calvert County?

Taxable increases on an owner-occupied home are capped at 10% a year effective July 1, 2026, if you have applied for the credit.

Can I get out of a Calvert County tax sale?

The Homeowner Protection Program can remove a qualifying owner from the tax sale process for three years. The county sets income, asset and assessed value limits.

Does a new Calvert County house carry an extra tax?

Yes. The county building excise tax on a new single-family detached house totals $12,950, paid in three installments, and it is a lien until paid.

Where is Worcester County, Maryland, and what is in it?

Worcester County is Maryland's only county on the Atlantic Ocean, in the far southeast corner of the state, and Snow Hill is the county seat. 695 square miles in total, 468 of them land, which makes it the second-largest Maryland county by total area. It is also the only one bordering both Delaware and Virginia.

The county was created in 1742 from Somerset County. The ground is flat and low, and the high point is only 49 feet, in the northwest near Route 12. Barrier islands, Fenwick and Assateague, shelter the coast. The Pocomoke River and its swamp run through the south.

The 2020 census counted 52,460 residents, with a median age of about 50.5. Towns include Ocean City, Berlin, Snow Hill and Pocomoke City, plus Ocean Pines, which is a census-designated place rather than a town.

How does Ocean City change the Worcester County housing picture?

Ocean City makes Worcester County unusual, because most of its homes are used seasonally. The 2020 census counted 30,028 housing units there and only 3,820 occupied year-round, with about 87 percent vacant, mostly seasonal use, according to the Ocean City article.

The resort sits on a barrier spit about 9 miles long and about 6.6 feet above sea level. Year-round population was 6,844 in 2020, but summer weekends bring 320,000 or more people. Condominium building boomed in the 1970s, with more than 15,000 units added.

What does the economy look like outside the resort?

Inland Worcester County runs on farming, poultry and small-town trades. Agriculture, seafood, timber and truck farming were the historic base, and large-scale poultry became a major industry after mid-century.

Pocomoke City grew around logging, shingle making and shipbuilding on the river. Berlin sits near the birthplace of naval officer Stephen Decatur. Public schools are run by Worcester County Public Schools, with Stephen Decatur, Snow Hill, Pocomoke and Worcester Technical high schools. Shore Transit and Ocean City's beach bus carry riders, and the nearest commercial airport is Salisbury-Ocean City-Wicomico Regional.

The 1962 Ash Wednesday nor'easter destroyed much of the residential development on Assateague Island and led to the national seashore and state park there.

The state Department of Assessments and Taxation reassesses property every three years, and owners get a notice with the old and new value. See the SDAT appeal page.

Owners may also qualify for credits. The Homeowner's Tax Credit depends on income and must be requested each year by October 1, and the county's Homestead Tax Credit appears automatically when an owner-occupied assessment rises past the set percentage.

Worcester County holds an annual tax sale of properties with unpaid taxes, and not receiving a bill is no excuse. The 2026 sale was set for June 9, according to the state schedule, and earlier sales were May 16, 2025 and May 17, 2024.

Where is Cecil County, and what is its terrain?

Cecil County is in the northeastern corner of Maryland, on the Delmarva Peninsula, bordering Pennsylvania and Delaware along the Mason-Dixon line. Its western edge follows the lower Susquehanna River and the northern coves and flats of the Chesapeake Bay.

The county covers 418 square miles, of which 346 are land and 72, about 17%, are water. The north is Piedmont hills and the south is Coastal Plain flatland, with elevations from sea level up to 534 feet.

The Elk River and the Chesapeake and Delaware Canal pass through the county, and Interstate 95 crosses it east to west. Elkton is the county seat and the largest town. The 2020 census counted 103,725 residents, and the 2025 estimate is 107,131.

What is the history of Cecil County, and why does it matter for older houses?

Cecil County was organized in 1674 and named for Cecil Calvert, the second Baron Baltimore. It was an early trading and shipping center, and the Principio Furnace exported pig iron.

Elkton sits at the head of navigation on the Elk River. Swedish mariners and fishermen settled the area in 1694 as Head of Elk, and the town was incorporated in 1787. In the 1920s and 1930s, Elkton was known as the elopement capital of the East Coast because of Maryland's looser marriage rules, with thousands of weddings a year.

In the 2020 census Elkton had 6,386 housing units with 6.9% vacant, so a seller there is not competing against a large pool of empty homes.

An owner can redeem until a court forecloses the right of redemption. A buyer may begin foreclosure six months and one day after the sale, and the county says it does not handle foreclosure itself. How is property tax assessed and billed in St. Mary's County?

The State Department of Assessments and Taxation values the property, and the St. Mary's County Treasurer sends and collects the bill at 23150 Leonard Hall Drive, Leonardtown. The Treasurer's office number is 301-475-4200, extension 3300.

The fiscal 2026 county real property rate is 0.8478. The county's tax bill estimator shows separate lines for county, state, fire tax, rescue and support, along with flat fees and a county homestead credit line.

  • Maryland reassesses each property every three years and spreads the increase equally over three years.
  • For state tax purposes, a home's annual assessment increase above 10% is not taxed. Counties can set a lower cap.
  • You can appeal a new assessment within 45 days of the notice date. The next steps are the Property Tax Assessment Appeals Board within 30 days of the final notice and then the Maryland Tax Court within 30 days of the board's order.
  • The county gets its tax file from the State on July 1, so ownership data updates once a year. Searching by address or parcel number is more reliable than searching by name.

What happens at the St. Mary's County annual tax sale?

The county holds its tax sale every year on the first Friday of March, covering the prior tax year. Owners of delinquent accounts are advertised in a local newspaper for four weeks before the sale. The most recent sale on the county page was held online on March 6, 2026, at 10:00 a.m.

The winning bidder receives a Certificate of Sale, which allows legal proceedings but does not give title or possession. If the owner redeems, the bidder gets back the taxes paid plus 6% annual interest through the month of redemption. If the owner does not redeem, the bidder may start court steps to foreclose the right to redeem. Properties are sold as is, and liens may survive the sale.

An owner who falls behind should treat the sale date as a hard deadline. Unpaid water and sewer bills, service charges and penalties are also first liens against the property, and MetCom handles those bills.

What costs and taxes come up when selling a St. Mary's County house?

Ask your settlement company about the county transfer and recordation taxes. The state's 2026 guide says St. Mary's County's transfer tax is limited by state law to 1%, with the first $30,000 of the buyer's principal residence price exempt, and that part of the recordation tax revenue goes to rural land conservation. It does not give the rate in force, so get that figure from the company handling your closing.

Also expect a payoff of any property tax due at settlement. The county posts bills and a payment portal online, and you can change a mailing address through the Treasurer's address change form. If back taxes are close to the tax sale, a cash offer with a quick closing can be a way to clear them, but compare it against a listing and ask for terms in writing.

What is the county seat of St. Mary's County?

Leonardtown is the county seat. California is the largest community, and Lexington Park is the other major population center near Naval Air Station Patuxent River.

What is the St. Mary's County property tax rate?

The fiscal 2026 county real property rate is 0.8478, according to the state's rate table. Your bill also shows state, fire, rescue and support lines, so the total depends on where the house sits.

When is the St. Mary's County tax sale?

The county holds its annual tax sale on the first Friday of March for the prior tax year. The 2026 sale was held online on March 6 at 10:00 a.m.

How do I appeal a St. Mary's County property assessment?

File within 45 days of the notice date with the local assessment office. Later levels are the Property Tax Assessment Appeals Board and the Maryland Tax Court, each with a 30 day window.

Do I need to test the well before selling a St. Mary's County house?

If the house has a private well, Maryland Real Property Section 10-713 requires the contract to call for water testing as a condition of sale unless the buyer waives it in writing. Test results are valid for three years.

Where is Talbot County, Maryland, and how is it laid out?

Talbot County sits on Maryland's Eastern Shore, with the Chesapeake Bay on its western side and Easton as the county seat. A total area of 477 square miles, but only 269 of those are land. The other 208 square miles, about 44 percent of the total, are water.

The county touches Queen Anne's County to the north, Caroline County to the east and Dorchester County to the south. The Choptank, Miles, Wye and Tred Avon rivers cut into the land, which is why so many Talbot County properties sit on a creek, cove or river frontage.

Five towns are incorporated: Easton, Oxford, St. Michaels, Trappe and Queen Anne, which is partly in Queen Anne's County. The 2020 census counted 37,526 residents, and the median age is about 50.7. U.S. Route 50 is the main highway. Talbot County Public Schools runs the public schools for the whole county, so a seller does not need to sort out separate school districts.

What does the Talbot County economy mean for a house sale?

Talbot County's economy leans on tourism, boating, financial services and health care, and that mix shapes who buys and who sells. Shore United Bank, headquartered in Easton, is described as the fourth-largest bank in the state, and Easton is treated as the financial center of the Eastern Shore.

Easton has a 112-bed hospital, the University of Maryland Shore Medical Center at Easton, and the town owns Easton Utilities, which supplies electricity, gas, water and wastewater. A newer regional health center is scheduled to open in Easton in 2028. For a homeowner, the practical effect is that town addresses often have town utility accounts and a town tax bill on top of the county bill.

  • Easton: the largest town, with 17,101 residents in 2020.
  • Oxford and St. Michaels: waterfront towns with their own municipal tax rates.
  • Trappe and Queen Anne: smaller towns along the Route 50 corridor.
  • Unincorporated areas: pay the county and state rates only.

Who handles property tax in Talbot County?

Two offices split the work: the county Finance Office bills and collects, and the state Department of Assessments and Taxation (SDAT) sets the value. The Finance Office is in the Talbot County Courthouse at 11 North Washington Street, Suite 9, Easton, and its main number is 410-770-8020.

When are Talbot County property taxes due?

Talbot County taxes are payable without interest as of July 1, and the deadline is September 30. Interest and penalties begin on October 1. According to the county tax sale page, the charge is one percent per month, or any part of a month, until the bill is paid.

Owner-occupied homes can pay in two installments, the first by September 30 and the second by December 31. A service charge applies to the second installment, and paying the full amount by September 30 avoids it. The county's rate page says the charge cannot exceed 1.279 percent of the unpaid December balance.

  • July 1: tax year begins and bills are payable.
  • September 30: last day without interest, and first installment date.
  • October 1: interest and penalties begin on unpaid taxes.
  • December 31: second installment for owner-occupied homes.

How are Talbot County assessments set, and how do you appeal?

SDAT reassesses each property on a three-year cycle and mails a Notice of Assessment showing the old and new market value. Notices for the 2026 reassessment went out on December 30, 2025, and SDAT's January 2026 report lists a residential value change of 18.2 percent for Talbot County. Increases in assessed value are phased in evenly over three years, while decreases take full effect right away.

An appeal must be filed within 45 days of the notice date. After that, the process has three steps:

  1. The supervisor's level, an informal talk with an assessor, often about 15 minutes.
  2. The Property Tax Assessment Appeals Board, which you can reach by filing within 30 days of the final supervisor notice.
  3. The Maryland Tax Court, with a further 30 days to file after the board's order.

A buyer who takes title between January 1 and July 1 has 60 days from the transfer to appeal, once the deed is recorded. Details are on the SDAT appeal page.

What happens if Talbot County taxes go unpaid?

Unpaid taxes become a lien on the property, and the county sells that lien at an annual tax sale. Under Tax-Property Article section 14-804, state, county and town real property taxes are a lien from the due date until paid.

The 2026 Talbot County sale was held on Wednesday, May 20, 2026. Earlier sales were June 9, 2025 and May 15, 2024, according to the state's tax sale schedule. A lien sale does not end the owner's right to redeem by paying the overdue taxes and fees, so a sale is a warning, not the final step.

Low-income homeowners may qualify for the Homeowner Protection Program, which can keep a home out of tax sale for at least three years and help with the balance. The State Tax Sale Ombudsman can be reached at 410-767-4994 or sdat.taxsale@maryland.gov.

What transfer and recordation taxes apply when you sell in Talbot County?

Selling a Talbot County house triggers a county transfer tax, a state transfer tax and a recordation tax. The county code sets its transfer tax at 1 percent of the consideration, with the first $50,000 exempt, and the Clerk of the Circuit Court collects it before a deed is recorded.

A Maryland law firm summary puts the recordation tax at 1.2 percent in Talbot County and the state transfer tax at 0.5 percent, for a combined 2.7 percent on deeds. When a first-time Maryland buyer purchases a principal residence, the state rate falls to 0.25 percent and the seller pays it. Who covers the other taxes is a matter for the contract. These rates change, so ask the title company for the exact figures on your settlement sheet.

Back taxes are paid from the sale proceeds at settlement, so an unpaid balance reduces what the seller receives.

Much of Talbot County is shoreline and farmland, so a buyer's lender may ask about the lot, access and any survey. Sellers who inherit a property often face a tax bill, a lien and an empty house at once.

Pay through the Finance Office in the Talbot County Courthouse, 11 North Washington Street, Suite 9, Easton, or online through the county's self-service portal. The office phone is 410-770-8020.

You have 45 days from the date on the Notice of Assessment. If you buy a house between January 1 and July 1, you have 60 days from the transfer, and the deed must be recorded first.
